title: Leases and the failure this system exists to prevent
summary: A lease ends when the job says so, when a deadline the user wrote down elapses, or when a human takes it back. Nothing else — not a socket error, not a probe timeout, not a device going offline, not a pod dying. The invariant is enforced in four independent places: a CHECK constraint with no word for connectivity, four guard-trigger rules, a Postgres role with SELECT revoked on the health table, and a one-way package dependency with a test behind it. All fifteen assertions in test/assertions.sql pass against a database migrated from this tree, and every example below was run against the live farm or a scratch database migrated from it. What is NOT enforced is named in Gaps: there is no host-side fence proxy, the max_runtime SWEEP ends a lease without fencing it, nothing produces a witness, farm.events is not a ledger of endings, and the API is open no matter what you set in the environment.

sections.heading: What a lease is
sections.body:
A lease is one row in `farm.leases`. It binds a **job** to a **device** at a **fence**, for a stated `ttl` and `grace`, and it is the only thing that grants the right to drive that device.

Ownership is keyed on `job_id`, not on the pod. `holder` is a pod name and is audit-only; `holder_instance` identifies one process incarnation and is what renew matches on. Two partial unique indexes make the arithmetic hold: `leases_one_live_per_device` and `leases_one_live_per_job`, both `WHERE state IN ('held','suspect')`. The schema comment says why the index and not the row lock is what prevents a double grant: under READ COMMITTED, EvalPlanQual re-checks quals only on the locked relation, so a subquery against leases still sees the original snapshot.

Four states, two of them live: `held` and `suspect` are LIVE; `released` and `expired` are terminal. A device is free when `devices.current_lease_id IS NULL`, maintained by the `leases_sync_device` trigger rather than by an anti-join.

One grep is worth more than the paragraph above: exactly one Go file outside `internal/lease` writes this table, and it is the operator revoke handler.
bullets: `protected` and `disruption_policy` are SNAPSHOTS copied from the job at acquire time (00002_lease.sql:274-284). Changing `jobs.protected` afterwards does not change a live lease.
`expires_at` and `reclaimable_at` are plain columns, not GENERATED — `timestamptz + interval` is STABLE, not IMMUTABLE, so Postgres rejects a generation expression.
`CHECK (reclaimable_at >= expires_at)` on the table: the grace band can be zero-width but never negative.

`jobs.ttl >= 10 minutes` and `jobs.grace >= 5 minutes` are CHECK-constrained (00001_core.sql:260-263). A config violating them fails every acquire with SQLSTATE 23514, which is why internal/config refuses to start instead.

The lease's ttl and grace come from the JOB ROW, not from the environment. `FARM_LEASE_TTL` / `FARM_LEASE_GRACE` are used only as defaults when a job is created through `POST /api/v1/jobs` (internal/api/jobs.go:297,:301). On this farm /capabilities reports 15m/30m while 1206 of 1222 leases actually ran at ttl 10m / grace 5m, because the demo creates its jobs with its own values.

No Go code in internal/lease binds a `time.Time` parameter. Every deadline is computed by Postgres against its own `now()`; durations cross the wire as interval literals in microseconds (`intervalArg`, store.go). Pod clock skew cannot expire a lease.

sections.heading: The three clocks, and what breaks when they are collapsed
sections.body:
Three different questions on three different clocks. DeviceFarmer/STF issue #663 fuses clock 3 and a transport failure of clock 1 into a release decision. That fusion is the entire bug: a ~90-minute ECONNRESET releases the device mid-run and destroys multi-hour work.

Here the three are separated by table, by function, by Postgres role and by Go package. There is no function in internal/lease that accepts an `io.Reader`, a `net.Conn` or an ADB handle — a socket error has no parameter to travel through.

rows: Does the entity holding this lease still exist?
Yes — via reclaim, after ttl+grace of silence, and only then
Is the work on the device making progress?
Not represented in internal/lease at all
Is this device reachable and usable?
device_runtime.adb_state / health, written by the watchdog
Never. Structurally unreadable to the reaper

bullets: Health IS an input to ALLOCATION (`lease_acquire` phase 2 requires `adb_state='device' AND health='healthy'`, 00002_lease.sql:239-240). It is never an input to RECLAMATION. That asymmetry is why one role cannot both have and not have `SELECT` on `device_runtime`, and why farm_reaper is a separate role.

internal/adbwire must not import internal/lease, internal/reaper, internal/scheduler, `database/sql` or pgx, and must contain no allocation vocabulary. `TestPackageCannotReachAllocation` (client_test.go:1022) scans every production file in the package and fails the build if any of that appears.

internal/obs closes the back door too: `obs.TransportBlip` is the only symbol adbwire may call, and it accepts no lease, job, fence or holder identifier and returns nothing, so there is no value for transport code to branch on (obs/metrics.go:472-486).
The node agent (internal/node) has no lease vocabulary and does not import internal/lease. It power-cycles USB ports UNDER live leases on purpose (agent.go:22-35).

sections.heading: The fence: what it protects, and where it is not checked
sections.body:
`leases.fence` is a monotonic `bigint` from `farm.fence_seq`, UNIQUE per lease. `devices.fence_floor` is the monotonic floor for that device. A live lease sits exactly AT the floor — the INSERT trigger does `fence_floor = GREATEST(fence_floor, NEW.fence)` (00002_lease.sql:141).

Ending a lease deliberately pushes the floor to a fresh `nextval()` ABOVE the fence it closed. That is what makes the previous holder's fence stale. `lease_release` (:406) and `lease_reclaim` (:568) both do it; the operator revoke does it in Go (api/leases.go:658); `lease_expire_max_runtime` does NOT.

The fence is checked in four places, and it is worth knowing which two do which job.
bullets: **Fence equality, against the lease row.** `farm.lease_renew` (:334) matches `(id, fence, holder_instance)`; zero rows is terminal for the caller. `farm.lease_release` (:397) matches `(id, fence)` and returns false on a mismatch — the idempotent case, not an error.

**Fence versus the device floor.** `farm.lease_witness` (:374) refuses when `l.fence < devices.fence_floor` — the comparison is `>=`, not `>`, precisely because a live lease sits AT the floor. `farm.device_state_write` (00004_operate.sql:455) refuses a durable device-state write below the floor, and refuses again on `written_by_fence` regression.

**NOWHERE ELSE.** Grep `fence_floor` across every .go file: `internal/api/fleet.go` reports it, `internal/api/leases.go` raises it on revoke, the rest are comments. No code path gates an ADB operation on it. The "refused at the host proxy" that three separate godoc comments promise does not exist in this tree — see Gaps.

sections.heading: The ending that cannot be written down
sections.body:
`farm.leases.release_reason` has a CHECK with exactly seven values (00001_core.sql:324):

`completed`, `failed`, `job_cancelled`, `max_runtime`, `operator_revoked`, `holder_expired`, `device_retired`

Read the list again for what is missing. There is no `device_offline`, no `transport_error`, no `unreachable`, no `probe_failed`. Connectivity has no word in this domain, so "released because the transport dropped" raises `check_violation` (SQLSTATE 23514) instead of silently destroying six hours of work.

The Go type `lease.ReleaseReason` mirrors the CHECK exactly, and `Store.Release` deliberately does NOT pre-validate. Neither does the HTTP handler — it requires the field to be non-empty and passes it through verbatim (api/leases.go:396-409, :433-438). The database is the enforcement point on purpose: a client-side allow-list would replace a loud, tested, server-side refusal with a quiet one. `ReleaseReason.Valid()` exists for callers building a reason from operator input who want to reject it early; nothing on the release path calls it.
bullets: If a transport failure genuinely ended your run, the honest reason is `failed` — the JOB failed. If it did not end the run, the honest response is to keep holding the device.
`holder_expired` is written in exactly one place in the whole tree: `farm.lease_reclaim` (00002_lease.sql:563). A live holder writing it would be lying about who gave up.

sections.heading: The guard triggers
sections.body: `leases_guard` is a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger (00002_lease.sql:95-133) enforcing four rules. Every one exists because a plausible-looking future edit would otherwise quietly destroy work.
bullets: **Identity is immutable.** `device_id`, `fence`, `job_id` and `acquired_at` cannot change on an existing lease. Note `acquired_at` is in that set — `max_runtime` is computed from it, so a mutable `acquired_at` would be a way to extend or shorten a user's deadline behind their back.

**`expires_at` never moves backwards.** Without this, a plain `now() + ttl` in a renewal silently erases a control-plane-gap refund. The SQL uses `GREATEST(l.expires_at, now() + l.ttl)`; the trigger is what stops a future edit from dropping the GREATEST.
**`reclaimable_at` never moves backwards.** Same reason.
**A terminal lease is terminal.** `released`/`expired` cannot go back to `held`/`suspect`. A resurrected pod cannot revive a lease that has already been handed on.

The trigger has a side effect worth knowing at 3am: you cannot force a lease into `suspect` by hand, because you cannot pull `expires_at` back into the past. To reproduce a reclaim you must insert a fresh lease row with past deadlines. This is also why assertion P10 does not test what its name says — see the assertions section.

sections.heading: The role firewall: health is UNREADABLE to reclamation
sections.body:
The draft design put `lease_acquire` and `lease_reclaim` in the same process, which voids the firewall: acquire MUST read `device_runtime` to allocate, reclaim must be unable to. One role cannot both have and not have that SELECT.

Resolution: `farm_reaper` is a distinct NOLOGIN role with `REVOKE ALL ON farm.device_runtime`, and `farm.lease_reclaim` carries a **function-level** `SET role = farm_reaper` (00002_lease.sql:533).

The mechanism detail matters. A function-level `SET` is saved on entry and RESTORED ON EXIT, so the role change is scoped to that function alone. `SET LOCAL ROLE` in the body would leak `farm_reaper` into the rest of the caller's transaction and the next unrelated statement would fail on a table the reaper cannot see. Assertion P15 tests exactly that, by calling `lease_reclaim` and then reading `farm.component_heartbeat` — a table the reaper's grant list does not include.

Note that the header comment at 00002_lease.sql:31 still describes the old `SET LOCAL ROLE` design. The function is what runs; the comment is stale.

This is not a style rule. No future edit to `lease_reclaim` can make releasing a device depend on whether that device is reachable, because the SELECT is not there to be written.
bullets: `GRANT farm_reaper TO farm_scheduler` (00002_lease.sql:87) exists only so the caller can `SET ROLE`. Membership does not weaken the firewall: SET ROLE REPLACES the active privilege set, so farm_scheduler's own SELECT on device_runtime is not in effect while the function runs.

The Go equivalent of the rule is simpler: `farm.device_runtime` is named nowhere in internal/reaper/reaper.go except in its own warning paragraph (reaper.go:34). Never add a health check in Go around `Store.Reclaim` — that rebuilds #663 on top of a schema built to prevent it.
The firewall is in force for `farm.lease_reclaim` and for nothing else — see Gaps. The grants on `farm_watchdog` and `farm_scheduler` are correct and unused.

sections.heading: held -> suspect -> held: suspect does NOT mean broken
sections.body:
When `expires_at` passes with no heartbeat, `farm.lease_mark_suspect` (00002_lease.sql:481) moves the lease from `held` to `suspect`.

Entering suspect **does nothing**. No reset, no reboot, no reallocation, no release. The device stays unschedulable and stays with its holder. `devices.current_lease_id` still points at the lease — the sync trigger only clears it on a transition INTO a terminal state.

A heartbeat anywhere in the grace band self-heals `suspect -> held` at the SAME fence with zero work lost. `lease_renew` sets `state='held'` unconditionally and reports the pre-image as `was_suspect`, computed from a sibling CTE because `RETURNING` yields the post-update row (so `RETURNING state='suspect'` would be a metric that silently reads zero forever).

Every suspect row is an alert. None of them is an action.
bullets: Holders in the shipped binary renew every 60s (`lease.DefaultRenewInterval`), so with a 15-minute TTL roughly fourteen consecutive renewals must fail before a lease even becomes suspect. A database that is down for ten minutes costs a running job exactly nothing. Note that `FARM_LEASE_RENEW_INTERVAL` does not change this — see Gaps.

internal/config refuses to start if `RenewInterval * 3 > TTL` (config.go:355-361): a holder must be able to lose two consecutive renewals — a rolling deploy, a Postgres failover, a long GC pause — without going suspect.
The suspect sweep is LIMIT-bounded (default 500) and uses `SKIP LOCKED`, so it is a fairness knob and not a correctness one.

There are zero suspect leases on this farm and there never have been, so `farm_lease_suspect` does not appear on /metrics at all — the gauge has no children until a census returns a row. Write your alert as `farm_lease_suspect{protected="true"} > 0` and accept that it is armed only from the first suspect, not from the first scrape.

sections.heading: Protected leases and 'hold and page'
sections.body:
A lease is `protected` if the job asked for it, OR if `jobs.expected_duration > interval '30 minutes'`. The rule is one line in `lease_acquire` (00002_lease.sql:275-276):

`v_protected := j.protected OR COALESCE(j.expected_duration > interval '30 minutes', false);`

`farm.lease_reclaim` has `AND l.protected = false` in its candidate CTE (:552). A protected lease that goes silent is NEVER automatically reclaimed. It sits in `suspect` indefinitely, holding its device, until a human resolves it.

This is a deliberate trade: a long job is exactly the job where an automatic reclaim is most expensive, so the system chooses to strand one device over destroying six hours of work. The cost is that a genuinely dead six-hour job parks a device until somebody notices — which is why the 'page' half has to actually exist, and here it does not.
bullets: Protection shields against the holder-silence path ONLY. `farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` has no `protected` filter and ends a protected lease like any other — verified, see that section.
An operator revoke also ignores `protected`. That is correct: a human taking a device back is one of the three legitimate endings.

'Page' today is a single WARN log line in `sweepSuspect` (reaper.go:336). The two metrics that were supposed to back it — `farm_reaper_suspect_marks_total{protection="protected"}` and `farm_lease_suspect{protected}` — are both absent from the running system's /metrics, for two different reasons. See Gaps.

sections.heading: The control-plane gap refund and the quiesce gate
sections.body:
Our downtime is refunded to tenants, never charged to them as lease budget.

`farm.reaper_arm` (00002_lease.sql:428) runs on every gain of leadership, BEFORE the first sweep. Sweeping first and arming second would reclaim exactly the leases the refund exists to save, so `cycle()` stands the reaper down entirely if arming fails (reaper.go:243-258).

It does two things:

1. **Gap refund.** It takes the OLDEST beat across `{reaper, api, scheduler}` — every component on the renewal path, not just the reaper's own. If that beat is older than the gap floor (60s), it writes a `control_plane_gap` row and adds the whole gap to `expires_at` and `reclaimable_at` of every live lease.
2. **Quiesce.** `quiesce_until = now() + COALESCE(max(ttl), interval '15 minutes')` over live leases. The delay derives from the longest TTL the reaper could have missed, not from a guessed constant. `lease_reclaim` returns immediately while `now() < quiesce_until`.

The multi-component gap is the BLOCKER-8 fix. Keying it on the reaper's own heartbeat alone is how a healthy reaper next to a dead API reclaims the entire farm: the reaper's beat is fresh, no gap is recorded, and after ttl+grace every unprotected lease in the farm is taken.
bullets: `lease_reclaim` ALSO refuses any lease whose silence overlaps a gap: `NOT EXISTS (gap WHERE g.ended_at > l.heartbeat_at AND g.ended_at > now() - interval '6 hours')`. Belt and braces — the refund moves the deadline, this clause blocks the reclaim outright.

Leader election uses a session advisory lock on a DEDICATED connection (`0x6661726d52656170`, which spells "farmReap"). Two reapers arming at once would refund the same outage twice; two restarting in a loop would extend every lease in the farm forever (reaper.go:551-561).

`FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS` must name every component on the renewal path; internal/config refuses to start a process whose role or FARM_COMPONENT is api/scheduler/reaper if it is missing from the list (config.go:409-418). It should NOT name the watchdog, the recovery ladder or the node agents — but nothing enforces that half. `farm.reaper_arm` ADDS each named component's downtime to every live lease, so letting a health-plane outage move lease clocks is the fusion this system exists to prevent, and it is one env var away.

The gap floor and the heartbeat interval are coupled: config refuses to start if `HeartbeatInterval * 2 > GapFloor`, or ordinary scheduling jitter is recorded as an outage and refunds lease time nobody lost.
`farm.control_plane_gap` is empty on this farm — no watched component has ever been silent for more than 60 seconds.

sections.heading: Witness extensions and their cap
sections.body:
A witness is on-device proof that the HOLDER is alive — a marker file touched by the holder's own agent — not evidence about device health. It buys a job that has lost its control-plane connection more room before the reaper will consider it.

Read the arithmetic precisely, because the godoc gets it wrong in two places. `farm.lease_witness` sets `reclaimable_at = GREATEST(l.reclaimable_at, now() + l.grace)`. That is a **floor, not an increment**. On a lease that is renewing normally, `reclaimable_at` is already `now() + ttl + grace`, so a witness moves nothing at all and still increments `witness_extensions`. It only buys time once the lease has drifted to within one grace period of being reclaimable — which is the regime it was written for, but not what "pushes reclaimable_at out by one grace period" describes.

It refuses when:

- `witness_extensions >= p_max_extensions` (default 12), so a wedged agent cannot hold a device forever on device-side evidence alone;
- the lease is not live;
- `l.fence < devices.fence_floor` — a stale witness from an already-fenced process. The comparison is `>=`: AT the floor is accepted, because a live lease always sits exactly there. (`internal/lease/store.go` documents this as "at or below", which is wrong.)

The cap counts only **consecutive** witness-only extensions. `lease_renew` sets `witness_extensions = 0`. Without that reset, a 12-minute job would exhaust the cap and the witness would protect nothing for the rest of the run (assertion P9).

A refused witness is NOT a fencing event and must never abort a job. Only `Renew` can report fencing.
bullets: internal/config refuses to start if `WitnessInterval * 2 > Grace` (config.go:363-369): `lease_reclaim` ignores any witness older than one grace period, so a witness landing less than twice per grace band protects nothing. That assertion guards a value nothing reads — see Gaps.
Nothing in this repository ever calls it. `Holder.Witness` has no caller outside internal/lease, and there is no API route.

sections.heading: Pod eviction: re-attach at the same fence
sections.body:
A Kubernetes pod eviction — node drain, preemption, spot reclaim, cluster upgrade, OOM restart — is the most ordinary event in a control plane and is not evidence that anything on the phone died.

`lease_acquire` is idempotent on `job_id`. Phase 1 (00002_lease.sql:206-230) looks for an existing lease for this job in `held` or `suspect` and hands it straight back. It updates `holder`, `holder_instance`, `holder_epoch + 1`, `heartbeat_at`, and pushes the deadlines outward with `GREATEST`. It **never bumps the fence**: the job's own work may still be running detached on the device, and bumping would fence out its own process.

The correct response to SIGTERM is therefore `Holder.Stop()`, not `Holder.Release()`. Stop cancels the holder's context so local work unwinds, and leaves the lease, the device and the fence exactly as they are. `Release` on shutdown would hand a half-finished job's device to somebody else. `internal/runner` follows this: on any cancellation that is not fencing and not max_runtime it sets `ReleaseReason = ""` and returns without touching the lease (runner.go:726-731).
bullets: A holder that sees `Reattached` must assume the device is DIRTY with its own prior state and resume from `jobs.checkpoint` rather than starting over. The API says so in the response body's `note` field.
`NewHolderInstance()` must be called ONCE per process incarnation. Re-minting it mid-run fences the process out of its own lease.

`holder_epoch` is the count of re-attachments and is the field to look at when asking "how many times has this job been evicted?". On this farm 1179 leases carry `holder_epoch > 0` and the maximum is 3 — the demo runs an eviction incident every 25 seconds on purpose.

Phase 2 (fresh allocation) re-checks its predicates under the row lock, because `ORDER BY` materialises the sort BEFORE locking so the locked row may no longer qualify. Rejected devices are accumulated in an array because `SKIP LOCKED` does not skip locks we ourselves hold.

sections.heading: max_runtime: two endings that look the same and are not
sections.body:
`max_runtime` is the one user-supplied clock allowed to end a lease automatically, because the user wrote the number down. It reaches the lease by TWO different paths, and the difference is whether the previous holder gets fenced.

**Path 1 — the holder notices.** `internal/runner` derives a relative deadline from what Postgres says is left of the budget, and on expiry releases with `ReasonMaxRuntime` through `lease.Store.Release`. That is `farm.lease_release`: state becomes `released`, `fence_floor` is raised to a fresh nextval, the slot is quarantined for rearm. Clean.

**Path 2 — the sweep.** `farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` (00002_lease.sql:591) is the safety net for a holder that did not notice — a wedged process, a crashed runner. It sets only `state`, `released_at` and `release_reason`. State becomes `expired`. The floor is NOT raised. The slot is NOT quarantined.

`state` is how you tell them apart, and on this farm both are happening: 19 `released`/max_runtime and 14 `expired`/max_runtime.

The sweep is the ending most likely to surprise you at 3am, for three verified reasons.

**It ignores `protected`.** There is no `protected` filter in the function.

**It does not fence.** The device is freed by the sync trigger and becomes immediately schedulable while the previous holder's fence is still AT (not below) the floor, so `farm.device_state_write` still accepts it.

**It is not gated by quiesce or by `reaper_state.enabled`.** Those gates live inside `lease_reclaim` only. A control-plane outage refunds `expires_at` and `reclaimable_at`; it does not move `acquired_at + max_runtime`. After a long outage, every job past its max_runtime is ended on the restored reaper's first sweep.

The window closes as soon as a new lease is granted on the device (the INSERT trigger raises the floor to the new fence), so the exposure is bounded — but it is exactly the window the 35-second slot rearm exists to cover elsewhere, and here there is no rearm either.

sections.heading: Renew: two outcomes that must never be swapped
sections.body:
`farm.lease_renew` is the only thing that keeps a lease alive. It takes no device lock, contacts no device, reads no health, and touches exactly one table. That path separation is the mechanism, not a happy accident.

It returns either one row or zero rows, and the difference is the single most consequential branch in the project:

**Zero rows = FENCED. Terminal.** One of four predicates failed — wrong fence, wrong `holder_instance`, terminal state, or the lease is gone. All four mean the same thing. Abort the job, close every ADB socket, write nothing. There is no retry and no grace; anything still in flight now belongs to somebody else's run.

**Any other error = TRANSIENT.** A dial failure, a timeout, a cancelled context, a failover, an exhausted pool. The lease is UNTOUCHED, no deadline moved, the device is still yours. Retry with jittered backoff and do not abort.

Getting this backwards in either direction recreates #663 — either by killing jobs on a database blip, or by letting a fenced process keep writing to a device that now belongs to someone else.
bullets: `Holder.Context()` is cancelled with `ErrFenced` as its cause, so every ADB socket, subprocess and worker derived from it unwinds at once. "Abort the job and close every socket" is one cancellation, not a checklist somebody has to remember.

`Holder.Fenced()` consults the loop's own recorded flag first and the cancellation cause second, because a concurrent Stop or Release can win the race to set the cause. "We were fenced" and "we shut down tidily" call for opposite responses.

`Holder.Release` cancels the context BEFORE issuing the release (release bumps the floor and starts the rearm window, after which the device can be handed on within seconds), then issues the release under `context.WithoutCancel` so the release survives the cancellation it just caused. An already-spent inherited deadline is dropped rather than re-imposed — otherwise a job torn down BECAUSE its deadline elapsed would fail to release and park the device for ttl+grace.

Backoff is jittered over the top half of the window. Every holder in the farm renews on the same cadence, so a database failover would otherwise synchronise thousands of retries against the instance trying to come back.
The HTTP mapping is 410 + code `fenced` versus 503 + code `transient` + `Retry-After: 2`. A holder that treats 503 as fencing is the bug.

sections.heading: test/assertions.sql — exactly what passed
sections.body:
Fifteen assertions. Every one raises an exception on failure, so a clean run is the proof. All fifteen passed.

The script cannot be run against the live `device_farmer` database: its fixture inserts `racks('r1')` and `hosts('h01')`, which the demo seed already owns, so it aborts at line 16. Run it against a database migrated from this tree instead.

rows: acquire grants a device and auto-protects a 6-hour job
pod eviction re-attaches the same lease at the same fence
a stale holder_instance renews zero rows; the current one renews one
expires_at is monotonic — a gap refund cannot be silently undone
lease identity (device, fence, job, acquired_at) is immutable
a device going offline + a suspect sweep leaves the lease untouched
a successful renew resets the witness extension counter
protected leases survive reclaim (hold and page)
ok, but it does not test that — see below
release bumps fence_floor, quarantines the slot, frees the device
a terminal lease cannot be revived
an API outage is recorded as a gap and quiesces the reaper
device health is UNREADABLE to the reaper role (insufficient_privilege)
lease_reclaim restores the caller's role on exit; it does not leak

bullets: **P10 does not exercise the protection branch.** It sets `heartbeat_at` back 10 hours but cannot move `expires_at` backwards (the guard trigger forbids it), so `lease_mark_suspect` matches nothing and the lease stays `held`. `lease_reclaim` only considers `suspect` leases, so it matches nothing either, and the final check `state IN ('held','suspect')` passes trivially. Replayed exactly: `mark_suspect matched 0 rows, reclaim matched 0 rows, state=held, expires_at 00:15:00 in the FUTURE`. Deleting `AND l.protected = false` from `lease_reclaim` would not fail the suite, because reclaim never reaches the protection test. The behaviour IS correct — proved separately by inserting leases with past deadlines (see 'Protected leases') — but this assertion is not what proves it.

P15 is subtle and worth keeping: it calls `lease_reclaim` and then reads `farm.component_heartbeat`, which is absent from farm_reaper's grant list. If the function used `SET LOCAL ROLE` in its body instead of a function-level `SET`, that second statement would fail.

protected          | f
disruption_policy  | allow_port_power_cycle
steps_done         | 0
steps_total        | 0
examples.note: Revoking closes fence 2329, raises fence_floor to the next sequence value, quarantines the slot for the configured 35s rearm, and writes rows to farm.audit_log and farm.events with your name and reason. `resumable=t` with `has_checkpoint=t` and `attempt < max_attempts` means the job can be re-run and will resume; `resumable=f` means the work is gone. Note the real row: `job_state=cancelled` while the lease is still held. Job state and lease state are separate — a cancelled job does not release its own device until its holder does.

examples.label: 4. What will the next sweep actually take? (the reclaim predicate, as a SELECT)
examples.code:
SELECT l.id AS lease_id, l.job_id, l.tenant_id,
       now() - l.heartbeat_at AS silent_for
  FROM farm.leases l
 WHERE l.state = 'suspect'
   AND l.reclaimable_at < now()
   AND l.protected = false
   AND (l.witness_at IS NULL OR l.witness_at < now() - l.grace)
   AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM farm.control_plane_gap g
                    WHERE g.ended_at > l.heartbeat_at
                      AND g.ended_at > now() - interval '6 hours')
 ORDER BY l.reclaimable_at;
examples.output: (0 rows)
examples.note: This is `farm.lease_reclaim`'s candidate CTE verbatim (00002_lease.sql:544-557), minus the quiesce gate that query 2 covers. Zero rows means the next sweep destroys nothing.

examples.label: 5. Has the control plane ever destroyed work on this farm?
examples.code:
SELECT state, release_reason, count(*), max(released_at) AS most_recent
  FROM farm.leases
 WHERE release_reason IN ('holder_expired','operator_revoked','max_runtime')
 GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
examples.note: `holder_expired` absent = zero reclaims, ever. That is the number to alert on: it counts work the control plane destroyed. Do NOT try to answer this from farm.events — that table records 0 lease_released and 0 lease_reclaimed rows against 1239 ended leases, because ordinary endings are not written there. See Gaps. For the one revoke, `SELECT detail FROM farm.events WHERE kind='lease_revoked'` does give you `revoked_fence` and `new_fence_floor`, and farm.audit_log gives you the human's name and reason.

sections.heading: Revoking: the human path
sections.body:
`POST /api/v1/leases/{id}/revoke` is operator-only, and it is the only ending where the decision is a person's.

It requires a `reason` and no fence. That asymmetry is deliberate: a holder must present its fence, a human must not have to. An operator taking a device back has no reason to know the holder's fence, and a revoke that needs the fence is a revoke that fails exactly when it is needed most.

It is written out longhand in the handler rather than going through `lease.Store.Release` for that reason — it is the one Go write path into `farm.leases` outside internal/lease. In one transaction (api/leases.go:610-705) it sets `release_reason='operator_revoked'`, raises `fence_floor` to a fresh `nextval`, quarantines the slot for the configured rearm, and writes both a `farm.audit_log` row (actor, reason) and a `farm.events` row.
bullets: The response carries `revoked_fence` and `new_fence_floor` so you can tell the old holder's support engineer exactly which fence died. The one revoke on this farm reads `revoked_fence: 1778, new_fence_floor: 1804`.
409 is an answer, not a crash — `farmd ctl` exits 3 for it (internal/ctl/ctl.go:44, :110-120). Exit 2 is a usage error.

**The API is open, and no environment variable closes it.** The live server reports `"auth":{"mode":"allow-all","open":true}` on `/api/v1/capabilities`, and its suggested fix ("set FARM_API_TOKENS") does not work: `cmd/farmd/roles.go:148` installs the allow-all authenticator unconditionally. Anyone who can reach :8420 can revoke any lease. Put it behind something else. See Gaps.

examples.label: The three ways the API says no
examples.code:
# already terminal
curl -X POST .../leases/8bef4852-0611-4f2e-a913-a046482cbf46/revoke -d '{"reason":"docs dry run"}'
# no reason given
curl -X POST .../leases/8bef4852-0611-4f2e-a913-a046482cbf46/revoke -d '{}'
# no such lease
curl -X POST .../leases/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/revoke -d '{"reason":"x"}'
examples.note: All three run against the live API; none ended a live lease.

examples.label: From the CLI, and how it refuses
examples.code:
export FARM_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8420
bin/farmd.exe ctl lease revoke <already-released-lease> --reason "docs verification" --yes
bin/farmd.exe ctl lease revoke <lease> --reason "docs" < /dev/null   # no --yes, no tty
bin/farmd.exe ctl lease revoke <lease> --yes                          # no --reason

lease; the request will be sent and the server will answer.

exit=3

examples.note: Run against the live API on an already-released lease, so nothing was destroyed. Note the CLI's pre-flight tells you the lease is not live and sends the request anyway — it does not pretend to know the server's answer. The warning banner about the host proxy is aspirational; see Gaps.

gaps.what: There is no host-side fence proxy. Every comment in the tree that says a stale socket is "refused at the host proxy" — lease/types.go:89 and :117, store.go:72 and :303, api/leases.go:578, and the `farmd ctl lease revoke` confirmation banner — describes something that does not exist. No Go file reads `devices.fence_floor` to gate an ADB operation (grep confirms: fleet.go reports it, leases.go raises it, everything else is prose), and internal/node serves only the two hardware recovery rungs. `FARM_NODE_SELF_FENCE_TIMEOUT` is validated by internal/config (SlotRearm must exceed it plus a margin) and has zero consumers anywhere else in the tree.
gaps.consequence: After a reclaim or a revoke, nothing severs the previous holder's in-flight ADB sockets. The device is protected only by (a) the 35-second slot rearm window and (b) the old holder noticing its own zero-row renew, which can take up to one renewal interval (60s). Between those, a fenced process can still be driving the phone, and the rearm window is shorter than the detection window. The database-level fence is real; the resource-level fence is not, and the operator-facing text says otherwise.

gaps.what: The API is open and cannot be closed by configuration. `cmd/farmd/roles.go:148` unconditionally appends `api.WithAuthenticator(api.NewAllowAll(log, "anonymous"))`. `api.AuthenticatorFromEnv` — the function that reads `FARM_API_TOKENS` and `FARM_API_AUTH` and would return a `StaticBearer` — has no caller in the tree. The live `/api/v1/capabilities` reports `"open":true` with the fix "set FARM_API_TOKENS to a token list", which does nothing.
gaps.consequence: Anyone who can reach :8420 is granted the operator role and can revoke any lease, drain any host and power-cycle any slot. Setting the documented environment variable creates a false sense of having closed it. The only real fix today is network-level, or building your own binary that calls `api.AuthenticatorFromEnv` or passes `WithAuthenticator(NewStaticBearer(...))`. Audit rows will read `actor=anonymous` for everything.

gaps.what: `farm.events` is not a ledger of lease endings. Measured on the live farm: 1239 leases have `released_at` set; `farm.events` holds 0 rows of kind `lease_released`, 0 of `lease_reclaimed` and 1 of `lease_revoked`. `lease_released` is written only by the API release handler (api/leases.go:527), and holders in this deployment release through `lease.Store` directly. `sweepMaxRuntime` writes no event at all. `lease_acquired` (1637 rows) is written only by internal/demo/demo.go:1117, not by production code.
gaps.consequence: A timeline query at 3am — "what happened to this device?" — silently under-reports. 33 max_runtime endings and 1225 releases left no trace in the table an operator would naturally reach for. The authoritative record of how a lease ended is `farm.leases.state` plus `farm.leases.release_reason`; treat farm.events as a partial commentary, not a log.

gaps.what: `farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` does not bump `fence_floor` and does not set `slots.rearm_at`, unlike `lease_release` and `lease_reclaim`. Verified: after a max_runtime sweep, fence 9 == fence_floor 9, slot rearm 00:00:00, device free, and `farm.device_state_write` then ACCEPTED a write from the ended holder at that same fence (revision 1). It also has no `protected` filter and is gated by neither `reaper_state.enabled` nor `quiesce_until` — verified by running it with the reaper disabled and quiesced an hour into the future.
gaps.consequence: A holder ended by the SWEEP path is not fenced and its device is schedulable the same instant with no quarantine. The window closes only when the next lease is granted on that device. Marking a job protected does not protect it from its own max_runtime. Turning the reaper off during an incident does not stop max_runtime endings. Note this applies only to the sweep: when the holder notices its own budget (internal/runner), it releases properly and everything is fenced — `state='expired'` versus `state='released'` is how you tell which happened, and on this farm both occur (14 and 19).

gaps.what: Nothing produces a witness. `farm.lease_witness` exists, `Store.Witness` and `Holder.Witness` exist, `FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_INTERVAL` and `FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_MAX_EXT` are loaded and validated — but `Holder.Witness` has no caller outside internal/lease, there is no API route, and no on-device agent touches a marker file. Neither witness config value has any consumer outside internal/config.
gaps.consequence: The extension that is supposed to protect a job which has lost its control-plane connection but is demonstrably alive on the device never fires. Across 1117 leases on this farm, `witness_at` is NULL on every one and `witness_extensions` has never exceeded 0. A long job that loses the control plane gets exactly ttl+grace and nothing more.

gaps.what: `FARM_LEASE_RENEW_INTERVAL` does not change the renewal cadence. `cmd/farmd/roles.go:420-435` constructs `jobrunner.Config` without a `HolderConfig`, so every holder falls back to `lease.DefaultRenewInterval` (60s). The configured value (default 90s) is validated at startup against the TTL and is echoed on `/api/v1/capabilities` as `"renew_interval":"1m30s"` — and is read by nothing else.
gaps.consequence: An operator who slows renewal down for a congested database changes a number on a status page and nothing else. The startup assertion that guarantees three renewal attempts inside the TTL is guarding a value no holder uses; the value they do use (60s against a 15m TTL) happens to satisfy it, but by coincidence rather than by check. The same is true of the witness-interval assertion.

gaps.what: There are no Go tests for internal/lease, internal/reaper, internal/scheduler or internal/api. The whole tree has seven `_test.go` files, all in internal/adbwire, internal/jobspec and test/fakeadb.
gaps.consequence: The ErrFenced-versus-transient branch in holder.go — the branch whose own doc comment calls it "the single most consequential decision in this project" — is untested. The `leaseOps` interface exists explicitly so a stub can drive that branch; nothing does. The lease protocol's only automated proof is test/assertions.sql, which tests the SQL and not the Go, and nothing runs even that automatically (there is no .github directory).

gaps.what: Assertion P10 ("protected leases are never auto-reclaimed") does not exercise the protection branch. It moves `heartbeat_at` back but cannot move `expires_at` back (the guard trigger forbids it), so `lease_mark_suspect` matches 0 rows, `lease_reclaim` matches 0 rows (it only considers `suspect`), and the final `state IN ('held','suspect')` check passes trivially. Replayed and confirmed: `mark_suspect matched 0 rows, reclaim matched 0 rows, state=held, expires_at 00:15:00 in the FUTURE`.
gaps.consequence: Deleting `AND l.protected = false` from `farm.lease_reclaim` would not fail the assertion suite. The behaviour is correct today — proved separately by inserting leases with past deadlines directly — but the regression test for the farm's most expensive failure mode is not actually watching it.

gaps.what: `reaper.Collectors()` is never called. No binary registers it; `internal/api/server.go:369` wires only `obs.Register` and `adbwire.Collectors()`. (The same is true of the Collectors() in internal/enroll, jobrunner, node, recovery, scheduler, topo and watchdog.) Confirmed against the live /metrics endpoint: no `farm_reaper_*` series at all.
gaps.consequence: `farm_reaper_leases_ended_total{reason="holder_expired"}` — the series the reaper's own documentation says to alert on, deliberately created at zero "so the alert is armed from the first scrape rather than from the first casualty" — does not exist on the running system. Same for `farm_reaper_leader` (whose sum across replicas must be 1), `farm_reaper_arm_failures_total` and `farm_reaper_sweep_errors_total`. Use `farm_lease_reaped_total{reason="holder_expired"}` from internal/obs instead; that one is registered and zero-filled.

gaps.what: `farm_lease_suspect` is absent from /metrics even though internal/obs is registered. `obs.Register` (obs/metrics.go:453-465) zero-fills only `leaseReaped` and `leaseRenewFailures`; the suspect GaugeVec gains children only when `SetLeaseSuspect` is called with rows, and this farm has never had a suspect lease.
gaps.consequence: `farm_lease_suspect{protected="true"} > 0` — the alert internal/obs/doc.go:43 tells you to write — cannot fire on a series that does not exist yet. It will start working the first time a lease goes suspect, which is also the first time you need it, so it is not fatal; but you cannot verify the alert is wired by looking for a healthy zero, and a dashboard panel for it will read "no data" rather than 0.

gaps.what: The role separation is only in force for `farm.lease_reclaim`. `farm_reaper`, `farm_scheduler` and `farm_watchdog` are created NOLOGIN with the right grants, but no Go code ever does `SET ROLE`, there is no per-component DSN, and deploy/helm is an empty directory. On the running system every component connects as `farm`, which is a SUPERUSER.
gaps.consequence: The reclaim firewall genuinely holds (function-level `SET role = farm_reaper` drops superuser for the duration — verified at 42501 from a superuser connection). But `REVOKE ALL ON farm.leases FROM farm_watchdog` protects nothing in practice: the watchdog process can write farm.leases because it is not running as farm_watchdog. The `has_table_privilege` query in this document tells you the grants are correct; it does not tell you anyone is using them.

gaps.what: `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS` is only half-enforced. internal/config refuses to start a process whose role or FARM_COMPONENT is api/scheduler/reaper if it is missing from the list (config.go:409-418), but nothing refuses ADDING a component. `farm.reaper_arm` adds each named component's downtime to every live lease's deadline.
gaps.consequence: Adding `watchdog`, `recovery` or `node:<host>` to that list — which looks like more thorough monitoring — makes a health-plane outage extend every lease clock in the farm. That is the exact fusion of clocks this system exists to prevent, and it is one environment variable away with no error and no warning. The prohibition is documented in reaper.go:110-119 and node/agent.go:36-45 and enforced nowhere.

gaps.what: `farm.reaper_state.enabled` is a global kill switch for the automatic release path, read by `lease_reclaim` on every call. No API route, no ctl command and no dashboard control sets it. (And it does not stop max_runtime — see above.)
gaps.consequence: Turning the reaper off in an incident means an `UPDATE farm.reaper_state SET enabled = false` by hand, with no audit row and nothing in the UI to show it happened. Turning it back on has the same problem. The reaper role has SELECT-only on this table, so the update must come from an ordinary connection.

gaps.what: No alerting rules, runbooks or pager integration ship with the tree. docs/ is empty, deploy/helm is empty, there is no .github directory. "Hold and page" is one WARN log line in `sweepSuspect` (reaper.go:336) plus two counters that are not exported (see the two metrics gaps above).
gaps.consequence: A protected lease that goes suspect is held indefinitely and correctly — and nobody is told. The reaper's own comment concedes this: it will sit there "until a human resolves it, which is correct and is also why nobody notices without a log line and the gauge behind it." You have to write the alert yourself, and today the only signals available on the running system are the log line and `protected_suspect` in the GET /api/v1/leases JSON.

gaps.what: test/assertions.sql cannot run against a seeded database. Its fixture inserts `racks('r1')`, `hosts('h01')`, `pools('default')` and `tenants('acme')`, all of which the demo seed already owns.
gaps.consequence: `make assertions DATABASE_URL=<the live farm>` aborts at line 16 with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "racks_pkey"` before a single assertion runs. Verifying the protocol against a production database means creating a scratch database and migrating it — which also means you are not verifying the database you actually care about.

gaps.what: Two godoc comments in internal/lease describe behaviour the SQL does not have. `store.go:280` says Witness is refused when "the fence is at or below the device's fence_floor" — the SQL requires `fence >= floor`, so AT the floor is the normal accepted case. `store.go:284-300` and the Witness section of holder.go describe the extension as pushing reclaimable_at "out by one grace period" when the SQL sets a GREATEST floor. Separately, the header comment at migrations/00002_lease.sql:31 still describes the old `SET LOCAL ROLE` design that the function no longer uses.
gaps.consequence: A holder written from the godoc rather than from the SQL would expect a witness on a healthy lease to buy time, and would expect a witness at its own fence to be refused. Neither is true. Read the function bodies.

- suspect self-heal: mark_suspect marked it, one lease_renew returned was_suspect=t and state back to held at the same fence 7.
- reaper_arm with a 25-minute-stale api heartbeat: both deadlines moved forward exactly 00:25:00, control_plane_gap row written for component "api", quiesce set to 00:15:00 (= max ttl).

The same call after a lease_release was REFUSED ("fence 11 is below the floor" against floor 12).

GREPS AND BUILDS: `go test ./internal/adbwire/ -run TestPackageCannotReachAllocation -v -count=1` PASS (0.718s). `find . -name '*_test.go'` -> 7 files, none under internal/lease, internal/reaper, internal/scheduler or internal/api. `grep -rn 'UPDATE farm.leases|INSERT INTO farm.leases' --include=*.go` -> one hit, internal/api/leases.go:626. `grep -rn fence_floor --include=*.go` -> no consumer that gates an ADB operation. `grep -rn '\.Witness('` -> one hit, inside holder.go. `grep -rn 'Collectors()'` -> only adbwire's is registered, at api/server.go:369. `grep -rn 'NewAllowAll|AuthenticatorFromEnv'` -> roles.go:148 only; AuthenticatorFromEnv has no caller. `grep -rn 'SelfFenceTimeout'` -> config only. `grep -rn 'Lease.RenewInterval|Lease.WitnessInterval|MaxWitnessExtensions'` -> capabilities.go reporting and jobs.go defaults only. `.github` does not exist; docs/ and deploy/helm/ are empty directories.

Live counters move between runs, so figures quoted from different examples were taken at different minutes on 2026-09-04 between 10:44 and 10:56.
